claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is single-phase and has a homogeneous microstructure containing nano-bridged dislocation channels.
Brittle behavior is triggered by a stress- or temperature-induced phase transformation.
The phase transformation produces discrete intermetallic precipitates at critical microstructural locations.
Discrete intermetallic precipitates disrupt nano-bridged dislocation channels.
Nano-bridged dislocation channels facilitate plastic deformation by allowing dislocations to move away from crack tips.
Nano-bridged dislocation channels contribute to crack blunting and toughness.
Restricting dislocation motion toward or away from a crack tip compromises fracture resistance.
Local compositional fluctuations or stress concentrations promote the proposed phase transformation under service conditions.
The resulting precipitates impede dislocation mobility away from crack tips.
Impeded dislocation mobility increases crack-tip stress concentration and promotes early crack initiation and propagation.
Low-temperature brittle behavior can occur in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Low-temperature cyclic loading is likely to activate diffusion-driven segregation or phase transformation.
Prolonged elevated-temperature exposure is likely to activate diffusion-driven segregation or phase transformation.
Thermally or mechanically cycled samples will develop intermetallic precipitates along nano-channels or related strategic regions.
Thermally or mechanically cycled samples will have lower fracture toughness, including lower KJIc, than the untreated single-phase baseline.
An intact nano-bridged dislocation network can provide an excellent combination of strength and toughness.
The proposed mechanism applies where transformation kinetics are activated but before complete microstructural degradation.
